904.title: Akiva's last Shema (Berakhot 61b)
904.hook: executed by Rome, Akiva dies saying the Shema, finally loving God "with all thy soul"
904.howItsDone: Jews say the Shema in the morning and evening prayers and at bedtime, with a custom of covering the eyes for the first line and lengthening the word echad, and it is traditionally said at the end of life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bar Kokhba, and a hope that failed. Your line was after the revolt. Today, what happened to Rabbi Akiva after it.

Rome has forbidden the teaching of Torah. Rabbi Akiva gathers students anyway, in public. A man named Pappos ben Yehudah asks whether he isn't afraid. Akiva answers with a parable. A fox by a river sees fish darting from place to place. Why are you running? From the nets, they say. Come up on the dry land, says the fox, and live with me. And the fish answer: if we're afraid in the water where we live, how much more on land, where we die. Torah, Akiva says, is our water. Not long after, he is arrested.
screen: `ROME FORBIDS TORAH.` → `THE FOX AND THE FISH.` → `TORAH IS OUR WATER.`

segments.voice: The Talmud tells what came next, in tractate Berakhot, page sixty-one. Akiva is taken out to be put to death, and the Roman executioners tear at his flesh with iron combs. It's the hour for the Shema, the verses from Deuteronomy said morning and evening: "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one." And Akiva says it. His students can't bear it: our teacher, even this far? Akiva answers, in paraphrase: all my life one phrase troubled me. The next verse says, "thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might." With all thy soul, the rabbis taught, means even if God takes your soul, your life. All my days I wondered when I would have the chance to keep this. Now that it has come, shall I not keep it? He draws out the last word of the first line, echad, one, and his life leaves him as he says it. The Talmud adds that a voice from heaven spoke: happy are you, Rabbi Akiva. The Talmud doesn't make it easy: in the same passage the angels protest: is this Torah, and is this its reward? But at its heart is a man who studied one phrase for years and, in the worst moment of his life, found that it fit. Akiva's last Shema is the ordinary Shema, said morning and evening in Jewish prayer, said all the way through.
screen: `THE HOUR OF THE SHEMA.` · `OUR TEACHER, EVEN THIS FAR?` · then, large: `WITH ALL THY SOUL.` · then: `HE DIES SAYING ONE.`

segments.voice: Sit tall; some people cover their eyes with one hand for the first line of the Shema, to shut out everything else. If you pray, say it slowly, Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one, and let the last word stretch the way Akiva stretched it. If you don't, hold the line as Akiva's words, and let your breath go long on that one word.
Echad. The Hebrew word for one, the last word of the Shema, which Rabbi Akiva drew out as he died under Roman torture.
Your line: with all your soul. Torah, Akiva said, was his water. Day nine hundred four, in the books.

905.title: The ten martyrs
905.hook: a Yom Kippur poem remembers ten sages killed by Rome
905.howItsDone: In synagogues, the poem Eleh Ezkerah is read during the Yom Kippur Musaf service, and a related lament for the martyred sages is said on Tisha B'Av.

segments.voice: Yesterday, echad: Rabbi Akiva said the Shema to the end and died on the word one. Your line was with all your soul. Today, Akiva is remembered again, in a poem, with nine others.

It's Yom Kippur. People have been fasting since the evening before. In the additional service, called Musaf, the room goes quiet for a long poem. It opens with two Hebrew words, eleh ezkerah: these I remember. Then it tells, one by one, how Roman authorities put ten sages to death. The words echo a psalm: "These things I remember, and pour out my soul within me." On the Day of Atonement, in the middle of asking for forgiveness, the congregation stops to remember.
screen: `YOM KIPPUR, THE ADDITIONAL SERVICE.` → `ELEH EZKERAH: THESE I REMEMBER.` → `TEN SAGES, ONE BY ONE.`

segments.voice: The poem frames it as a single decree. A Roman ruler reads in the Torah that kidnapping a person and selling him is a crime punished by death, and he remembers that Joseph's brothers sold Joseph. Since the brothers are long gone, he demands ten sages in their place. Rabbi Yishmael, the poem says, purifies himself and ascends to heaven to ask whether the decree truly comes from above, and he is told to accept it. Then the names. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. Rabbi Yishmael. Rabbi Akiva, whose death we heard yesterday. Rabbi Chanina ben Teradion, who taught Torah in public with a scroll in his lap. The Talmud, in tractate Avodah Zarah, tells that he was burned wrapped in that scroll. His students asked what he saw, and he answered, in paraphrase: the parchment is burning, and the letters are flying up into the air. Some readers point out that the rabbis' own stories place these deaths at different times, not on one day. The poem gathers them anyway. It isn't a court record. It's a liturgy of memory, setting ten people in a row so a congregation can hold them together. A related lament is also said on the ninth of Av. And on Yom Kippur, the remembering sits inside the prayer, not beside it.

If you pray, you can say a psalm you know in their memory.

906.title: Judah the Prince
906.hook: Rabbi Judah, called simply Rabbi, gathers the oral teaching into the Mishnah
906.howItsDone: The Mishnah attributed to Rabbi Judah the Prince is the foundation text of the Talmud, studied in yeshivas, synagogues and homes, and some learners take a little each day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, eleh ezkerah, and a scroll whose letters flew up from the fire. Your line was the ten. Today, a teacher makes sure the letters land somewhere safe.

One word, with no name after it: Rabbi. That's how the Talmud can refer to Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi, Judah the Prince. Just Rabbi. Nasi means prince, or leader, and he led the Jewish community of his day. But his lasting work wasn't politics. It was a book. For generations, the sages' teachings had been passed on by mouth, teacher to student, memorized and repeated. Rabbi gathered them and set them in order. The result is called the Mishnah.
screen: `CALLED SIMPLY: RABBI.` → `NASI: THE PRINCE, THE LEADER.` → `HIS LASTING WORK: A BOOK.`

segments.voice: Here's the tension. The rabbis had a rule, recorded in tractate Gittin: words given orally, you may not say from writing. The Oral Torah was meant to live in memories, in the back and forth between teacher and student, and writing it down risked freezing it. So how could anyone write it down? The Talmud answers with a verse from the Psalms, read in a daring way: "It is time for the LORD to work; they have made void Thy law." There are times when, to protect the Torah, you have to do what is normally not done. Maimonides gives Rabbi's reason: students were growing fewer, troubles kept coming, and teaching that lived only in memory could be lost. The tradition itself disagrees about exactly what Rabbi did. Maimonides wrote that he compiled the Mishnah and wrote it down. Rashi held that he arranged it and fixed its wording, but that it was still learned by heart, and only written later. Both agree on the heart of it: Rabbi gave the teaching an order. He didn't erase the arguments. The Mishnah keeps the house of Shammai beside the house of Hillel, names who said what, and records minority views. He organized without silencing. And the Talmud remembers him as a person, not only an editor: a story in tractate Bava Metzia tells that he once spared a family of small animals his maid wanted to sweep away, quoting the psalm: "His tender mercies are over all His works."
screen: `ORAL WORDS, NOT TO BE WRITTEN.` · then, large: `A TIME TO ACT FOR THE LORD.` · `MAIMONIDES AND RASHI DISAGREE.` · then: `ORDER WITHOUT SILENCING.`

segments.voice: Picture one small thing in your life that's scattered: a pile of papers, a phone full of notes, a family recipe that lives only in one person's head. Imagine it gathered and ordered, nothing important thrown out, every voice still in it, and let the first small step become clear. If you pray, you can offer that work as the rabbis offered their study.

907.title: The Mishnah
907.hook: six orders of oral teaching, written down so they wouldn't be lost
907.howItsDone: Jews study Mishnah in small portions, and some learn a chapter in memory of someone who has died; it is studied in yeshivas, synagogues and at home, often aloud with a partner.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nasi: Judah the Prince gave the oral teaching a shape. Your line was writing it down. Today, we open what he made.

The book begins with a question, and not a grand one. From when may a person recite the Shema in the evening? No creation story. No hero. Just a practical question about a prayer said every night, and right away three answers: Rabbi Eliezer says one thing, the sages another, Rabban Gamaliel a third. Then a little story. Gamaliel's sons come home late from a wedding feast and tell their father they haven't said the Shema yet. The night is far along. Is it too late? That is how the Mishnah opens: a family, a late night, and a room full of teachers who don't all agree.
screen: `FROM WHEN, IN THE EVENING?` → `THREE ANSWERS.` → `SONS HOME LATE FROM A WEDDING.`

segments.voice: The Mishnah is teaching that tradition calls oral Torah: the explanation that, in Jewish belief, traveled alongside the written Torah, taught teacher to student and learned by heart. Tradition ties the name to a Hebrew word for repeating, because it was learned by saying it over and over. Now it is written. Six orders, each called a seder. The Talmud later finds all six in a single verse of Isaiah, one word for each: seeds and farming, appointed times and festivals, women and marriage, damages, holy things, and purities. Inside the orders are tractates, inside the tractates chapters, and inside each chapter short units, each also called a mishnah. So the word names the whole book and one small piece of it. What surprises a first reader is that the Mishnah keeps the minority opinion. Back to that first page. The sages say the evening Shema may be said until midnight. Rabban Gamaliel says until dawn. So when his sons come home late, he tells them: if the dawn hasn't come up, you are still obliged to say it. And the page records both views, with names attached. Disagreement isn't erased when the teaching is written down. It's kept, carefully, as part of the teaching. The oral, written, still sounds like people talking.
screen: `ORAL TORAH, NOW ON THE PAGE.` · `SIX ORDERS, FOUND IN ONE VERSE.` · then, large: `THE MINORITY VIEW IS KEPT.` · `GAMALIEL: UNTIL DAWN.`

segments.voice: Here is the first mishnah in plain words. From when may the Shema be said in the evening? From the hour the priests go in to eat their holy portion; until when? Rabbi Eliezer says until the end of the first watch of the night, the sages say until midnight, and Rabban Gamaliel says until dawn. Hold the three answers side by side, nobody erased, and if you pray, say a short evening prayer you know; if not, rest with the question: what in your life is still not too late?
Mishnah. The oral teaching, written down and arranged in six orders. The word names the whole book, and also each short unit inside it.
Your line: the oral, written. Three answers on one page, and every one kept. Day nine hundred seven, done.

908.title: The Jerusalem Talmud
908.hook: sages in Galilee complete a Talmud, the teaching of the land itself
908.howItsDone: The Jerusalem Talmud is studied in yeshivas and by individuals alongside the Babylonian Talmud, and is turned to especially for the farming laws of the land of Israel.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mishnah: three answers about the evening Shema, and Gamaliel's sons home late from a wedding. Your line was the oral, written. Today, sages who counted stars.

One star in the sky: it's still day. Two stars: nobody's sure. Three stars: now it's night. That rule of thumb comes from a conversation about yesterday's question, when the evening Shema may begin. The Mishnah said the time starts when the priests go in to eat their holy portion. But what if you're standing outside, with no priest in sight? You look up and count. The sages who counted the stars lived in the land of Israel itself, in towns around the Galilee. What they built is known by a name that points somewhere else entirely.
screen: `ONE STAR: DAY.` → `TWO STARS: UNSURE.` → `THREE STARS: NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Once the Mishnah was written, students did what students do: they asked questions of it. Why does this teacher say midnight? What's the source in the Torah? What if the case is a little different? Their long, recorded discussion of the Mishnah is called Gemara, and Mishnah plus Gemara together is a Talmud. There are two. Today's is usually called the Jerusalem Talmud, in Hebrew the Yerushalmi. But its sages taught in the Galilee, not in Jerusalem. Its older names say where it came from: the Talmud of the Land of Israel, the Talmud of the West. You can feel the land in it. It has Gemara on the order of Seeds, the farming laws: tithes, the corner of the field left for the poor, the seventh year when the land rests. Laws tied to the soil of the land, discussed by sages who lived on it, in a language close to the Aramaic spoken around them. Some readers notice something else. The Yerushalmi can be terse. Arguments start and stop; a question is raised and the page moves on. Some readers sense a work that was never fully smoothed out. Students still learn it, unfinished edges and all, reading closely what is there.
screen: `MISHNAH PLUS GEMARA IS A TALMUD.` · `NAMED FOR JERUSALEM, MADE IN GALILEE.` · then, large: `THE TALMUD OF THE LAND OF ISRAEL.` · `TERSE, WITH UNFINISHED EDGES.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something left incomplete: a project you set down, a letter never sent, maybe something someone you love began and didn't finish. Don't fix it or judge it; look at it the way students read the Yerushalmi, as worth learning from exactly as it is, and ask what the unfinished part tells you that a polished version wouldn't. If you pray, you can give thanks for work that was begun.

909.title: Sura and Pumbedita
909.hook: the great academies of Babylonia become the center of learning
909.howItsDone: Jewish study still often happens in a yeshiva or study hall, and some communities hold gatherings for adult learning inspired by the old kallah months of Babylonia.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Yerushalmi, made in the Galilee: one star is day, three stars are night. Your line was the land's talmud. Today, we travel east, to the rivers of Babylon.

Maybe you're from Pumbedita, where they pass an elephant through the eye of a needle. That's the Talmud's teasing reply to an argument a little too clever. Pumbedita was a town in Babylonia, and apparently its scholars had a reputation: they could make anything fit through anything. It's a joke, with a compliment hiding inside. To earn a name like that, a town needs a lot of people arguing about texts for a very long time. So where were they, and how did a school in Babylonia end up with that kind of name?
screen: `AN ELEPHANT THROUGH A NEEDLE.` → `A JOKE ABOUT PUMBEDITA.` → `WHERE DID THESE SCHOLARS COME FROM?`

segments.voice: Babylonia, the land between the rivers, had a Jewish community from the time of the exile. Psalm 137 remembers it in grief, in the 1917 Jewish translation: "By the rivers of Babylon, There we sat down, yea, we wept, When we remembered Zion." Centuries later, that land of weeping became a place of learning. Two towns stand out in the story: Sura and Pumbedita. Each had its academy, a yeshiva, with a head, students, and a way of reading the Mishnah all its own. Tradition tells that Rav, a student who had learned in the land of Israel, came down to Babylonia and taught at Sura. The elephant joke suggests Pumbedita had a name for clever argument. The Talmud also speaks of public gatherings for learning called the kallah, where crowds came to listen, and it has a line about that crowd: the reward for attending the kallah is the crowding. You're packed in, elbow to elbow, and that is the point. Learning moves. It doesn't belong to one city. The conversation that began in the land of Israel went on by other rivers, as people carried the Mishnah in their memories and their scrolls, and opened new rooms to argue in.
screen: `BY THE RIVERS OF BABYLON.` · `TWO ACADEMIES: SURA AND PUMBEDITA.` · then, large: `THE REWARD IS THE CROWDING.` · `LEARNING MOVES.`

segments.voice: Think of the places you actually learn: a kitchen table, a bus seat, a library, a friend who explains things well. Pick one, see it clearly, and ask what would make it a better room for learning, a book left out, a regular time, another person to learn with; the academies were people as much as buildings. If you pray, you can ask for a place and a partner to learn with.

910.title: The Babylonian Talmud
910.hook: the academies' long conversation is gathered and sealed into the Talmud studied today
910.howItsDone: Jews study the Babylonian Talmud in yeshivas and study halls, often in pairs called chavruta, and some follow Daf Yomi, a cycle of one page a day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, yeshiva: the academies of Sura and Pumbedita, where scholars could pass an elephant through a needle. Your line was learning moves. Today, what those academies left behind.

Where is the teacher standing? That is the first question of the Babylonian Talmud. It copies out the Mishnah's opening line, the one we read this week: from when may the Shema be said in the evening? And before answering, it pushes back. Who said there is any duty at all? Where does this come from? Then it answers itself with a verse of the Torah, which in the 1917 Jewish translation says to speak of these things "when thou liest down, and when thou risest up." The Mishnah opened with a question. The Talmud opens with a question about the question.
screen: `WHERE IS THE TEACHER STANDING?` → `WHERE DOES THIS COME FROM?` → `A QUESTION ABOUT THE QUESTION.`

segments.voice: The Babylonian Talmud, the Bavli, is the record of the academies we met yesterday: generation after generation of Babylonian sages questioning the Mishnah, line by line. It's mostly in Aramaic, the everyday language of those rooms, with the Mishnah's Hebrew quoted piece by piece. It argues. It tells stories. It wanders into dreams, medicine and the rain, then comes back to the law. Like the Mishnah, it keeps views that did not win, with names attached; even its first page gives two answers to one question and keeps both. Then the book was closed. The Talmud names the moment in one brief sentence: Rav Ashi and Ravina are the end of instruction. Tradition reads that as the sealing. Later teachers would explain and rule, but they would not add to the Talmud. Sealed doesn't mean finished with. It means a fixed text, so that everyone after could open the same page and argue about it together. Now step back over this week. Akiva saying the Shema with his last breath. Eleh ezkerah. Nasi writing it down. The Mishnah. The Talmud of the land. The academies by the rivers. And now the Bavli: a people losing its Temple and its land, and building a book you can carry anywhere.
screen: `THE RECORD OF THE ACADEMIES.` · `IT KEEPS THE LOSING SIDE.` · then, large: `RAV ASHI AND RAVINA: THE END.` · `A BOOK YOU CAN CARRY ANYWHERE.`

segments.voice: On that same first page, the Talmud asks why the Mishnah speaks of evening before morning. One answer is the verse itself, which puts lying down before rising up; the other reaches back to creation, where, in the 1917 Jewish translation, "there was evening and there was morning, one day." Evening first: in this reading, a day begins as the light goes, with rest, so breathe slowly and think of this evening as the start of tomorrow. If you pray, you can give thanks, in words you know, for the day that is ending.
Bavli. The everyday name for the Babylonian Talmud, the academies' long argument over the Mishnah, mostly in Aramaic, closed with Rav Ashi and Ravina.
